title: Al-Wahhab, the Bestower
hookLine: the Bestower, who gives without asking a return
tomorrow: Dadi says count what's been provided. where do you even start?

lines: A GIFT THAT ASKS NOTHING BACK?
cards: A gift can come with a gift receipt tucked inside, or with an invisible one: you'll owe me. Yesterday's question was about the other kind.
Jordan's grandmother, Miss Loretta, brought over the paint left from repainting her church hall, and wouldn't take a dollar for it. Why give like that?
One question for today, then: what does a gift that asks nothing back look like?

teach.b: Islam's answer starts with a name: al-Wahhab, the Bestower, who gives without asking a return.
The Qur'an puts it inside a prayer believers say, asking that their hearts not stray and for mercy from His presence, ending: "Lo! Thou, only Thou, art the Bestower." Only Thou.
A human gift usually carries a hope: thanks, a favor later, at least being liked. Al-Wahhab needs nothing from anyone.

teach.h: NO REWARD NOR THANKS FROM YOU.
teach.b: And the Qur'an describes people who try to give in that same spirit, feeding the hungry and saying: "We wish for no reward nor thanks from you." Now the neighbor. Miss Loretta's church reads the same idea in its own book.
In the Gospel of Matthew, Jesus sends his followers out to heal, and tells them, in the King James words: "freely ye have received, freely give."
Here's what the two share: a gift passes on easily when the giver remembers it was first given to them. The paint came from somewhere before it came to Amira's wall. And here's an honest difference.
Christians hear Jesus's line inside their faith in him, whom they call the Son of God.
In Islam, Jesus is honored as a prophet, and al-Wahhab is a name for God alone, the Giver behind every giver, with no one standing in between.
Two houses, two ways of telling it, one thing worth saying to a friend tonight: the freest gifts come from people who know they've been given to.

how: Muslims recite the Qur'anic prayer of surah Al 'Imran 3:8, which ends by calling on al-Wahhab, and charity given in secret, wanting no thanks, is praised in the tradition.

o: the One who repays every good deed in kind
the One who sends gifts to the deserving few
the One who gives freely and asks no return

games.q: the gift with no strings — tap the pairs.
p: the end of a Qur'anic prayer
Jesus to his followers, in Matthew
what the givers in the Qur'an ask

s: a gift isn't really a gift unless the person pays you back somehow
the givers in the Qur'an say: we wish for no reward nor thanks from you.
Christians and Muslims both have scripture about giving because you've received
freely ye have received, freely give, in Matthew; al-Wahhab, the Giver behind every giver, in the Qur'an.
Islam and Christianity understand Jesus the same way
Christians call him the Son of God; in Islam he is honored as a prophet. the shared idea of giving doesn't erase that.

games.q: a neighbor fixes your bike and waves off any payment. you feel weird owing her. what fits today's lesson?
o: thank her warmly, and pass a free gift on to someone else.
insist on paying, so nobody owes anybody anything at all.
say nothing, since thanking her would turn it into a trade.
games.why: thanks doesn't cancel a gift. passing it on is what both Matthew's line and the Bestower's name point toward.

practice: Choose one small thing you could give today with no way to be paid back: a snack left on a coworker's desk, a bill in a donation box, a compliment with your name left off.
Hold it in mind through the sit, and each time a little you'll-owe-me slips in, let it go.

wordCard.voice: Al-Wahhab: the Bestower, who gives freely and asks no return. In the Qur'an's prayer: only Thou art the Bestower.

orig.note: Arabic: the Bestower, who gives freely. in the prayer of Qur'an 3:8.

carryVoice: Worth keeping: freely given, freely passed on, no receipt inside. That's six names this week.
